title: Use a butane cassette stove without burns, fire or CO
summary: A cassette stove cooks on an 8 oz (227 g) butane can and is the easiest burner to run in a winter outage. The can lies in a bay beside the burner and explodes when an oversized pot, a griddle, an upside-down grate or a second stove heats it. Like every flame it makes carbon monoxide: if its label allows indoor use, cook with a window open and a CO alarm, and if the label says outdoor only, use it outside. Never use it to heat the room.

materials.item: Cassette (tabletop) butane stove, checked for rust and damage
Butane cassette cans of the type the stove names

materials.qty: 1 in the room, 1 outside sleeping areas

materials.item: Pot or pan no wider than the stove grate
Soapy water and a small brush for leak checks

steps.text: Read the labels on the stove and the can. If the label says outdoor use only, use it outdoors: the camp-stove standard these stoves are certified to covered outdoor use only when CPSC reviewed it, and CDC says never to use a camping stove inside a home, tent or camper (CPSC butane report, Health Canada butane, CDC power outage). Look the body over: a rusty, dented or bent stove goes in the scrap pile.
steps.warn: A man in Hong Kong was treated for CO poisoning in July 2026 after cooking on a badly rusted cassette cooker; the rust is believed to be the cause and no gas leak was found (HK CO case 2026).

steps.text: Set it on a flat, steady, non-combustible surface. Keep it off and away from other stoves, hot plates, wood-stove tops and heaters, and never run two cassette stoves side by side (Health Canada butane, Tiger cartridge stoves, EMSD cassette leaflet).
steps.warn: Two stoves side by side were involved in 4 of the 14 incidents CPSC investigated (CPSC butane report).

steps.text: Turn the grate and drip pan the right way up, pot supports pointing up. Many stoves are packed with it upside down (Health Canada butane, CPSC butane report).
steps.warn: An upside-down grate throws flame back at the stove; in CPSC tests it heated the regulator to 74–109 °C (CPSC butane report).

steps.text: Choose a pot or pan no wider than the grate. Nothing may hang over the canister bay: no griddles, plancha plates, stone plates or big woks (Health Canada butane, EMSD hot pot). Don't wrap foil on or around the burner, or use the stove in any way that traps heat (SG CPSO butane tips).
steps.warn: A griddle over the bay raised the regulator to 75–118 °C in CPSC tests and set off the pressure cut-off (CPSC butane report).

steps.text: Check the can for damage, and that it is the type your stove names (EMSD hot pot, Tiger cartridge stoves). Look at the stove's O-ring or seal: it should be in place with no visible cracks or damage (ESV butane).

Fit the can outside or by an open window, away from any flame and other people (Jetboil Flash). Face its coupling recess up, line up the cutout with the guide in the bay, then push the lever down to the loaded position (Tiger cartridge stoves, EMSD hot pot).
steps.warn: A can that sits crooked leaks at the joint, and that gas lights (Health Canada butane, ESV butane). If it won't lock, don't force it and light anyway: one such can exploded five minutes later (CPSC butane report).

steps.text: Listen and smell. A hiss or gas smell means lift the lever and take the can out at once (Tiger cartridge stoves). Brush soapy water on the joint if you can see it: growing bubbles mean a leak (ESV butane). Never look for a leak with a flame.

If the label allows indoor use and you are cooking inside, open a window near the stove and keep a battery CO alarm in the room, with another outside the sleeping rooms (Health Canada CO). Run the range hood fan if you have power (Health Canada cooking), or an exhaust fan (HK CO case 2026).

Close the bay lid and turn the knob to light, then put the pot on. If it hasn't lit within about 5 seconds, turn it off and wait 5 minutes for the gas to clear before trying again (Jetboil's rule for its own canister stove).

Stay with it while it burns (EMSD hot pot), and turn it off as soon as the food is done. Never leave it running to warm the room (CDC power outage). In normal use the can runs cooler than the room (CPSC butane report), so a bay that is getting hot is a warning.
steps.warn: If the bay gets hot or the flame roars and won't turn down, turn the knob off from the side and step back. See When no help is coming.

steps.text: In the cold, keep the can inside your coat or sleeping bag until you cook, and don't leave it on snow or cold metal (Jetboil FAQ). Butane boils at about 0 °C (32 °F), so a plain butane can gives little gas near freezing (NIST butane, Jetboil FAQ).
steps.warn: Warm a can with body heat only. Jetboil says never to warm a can with the stove because it can explode (Jetboil Flash); a flame or heater is the same risk.

steps.text: When done, turn it off, let it cool, and take the can out. Store cans upright somewhere cool, dry and ventilated, away from flames and heat (EMSD hot pot, Jetboil Flash).

notes:
## What it is

A cassette (tabletop) stove is a flat single-burner cooker with an 8 oz (227 g) butane can lying on its side in a covered bay next to the burner. The can's nozzle plugs into a regulator, sealed by an O-ring, and is held by a lever or a magnet. A piezo spark lights it when you turn the knob, and the regulator has an over-pressure cut-off (CPSC butane report). Restaurants use them for buffets and table cooking, and they are sold as backup stoves for power failures. Depending on the flame setting, one can lasts 1 to 5 hours (CPSC butane report).

## Why the canister bay explodes

Health Canada's 2021 advisory is about exactly this design: the can lies flat inside the stove body, overheats, and either bursts or vents gas that catches fire (Health Canada butane). The causes keep repeating:

- **Cookware that covers the bay.** A griddle, plancha, stone plate or big pan reaches over the can, traps heat and blocks the air. In CPSC's lab tests the regulator ran at 34–71 °C (88–160 °F) with a normal pan, but 75–118 °C (162–244 °F) with a griddle over the bay, and the pressure cut-off tripped in three griddle tests (CPSC butane report). Hong Kong's gas regulator says the same in one line: no pot or plate big enough to cover the cylinder box (EMSD hot pot).
- **The grate upside down.** Many stoves ship with the grate and drip pan inverted to save space. Used that way, the flame is thrown back onto the stove. CPSC found inverted grates behind several incidents, and in tests the regulator reached 74–109 °C (165–228 °F) (CPSC butane report).
- **Two stoves side by side, or a stove on or next to another heat source** (Health Canada butane, Tiger cartridge stoves, EMSD cassette leaflet). Of the 14 incidents CPSC investigated, four involved two stoves side by side and four an inverted grate (CPSC butane report).
- **A can that isn't seated right,** so gas leaks at the joint and lights (Health Canada butane, ESV butane).

In nearly all of CPSC's investigated cases the can's own rim vent had opened, which means the bay had got far too hot (CPSC butane report). The usual story: the stove had been on for at least five minutes, then a bang and flames shooting upward, sometimes as high as 1.8 m (6 ft). In one case the user struggled to lock a fresh can into place, got it lit, and it exploded five minutes later (CPSC butane report). Those 14 incidents caused 24 burn and impact injuries (CPSC butane report).

Don't count on the cut-off. Recalls keep coming: in November 2025 about 201,000 Ozark Trail tabletop butane stoves sold at Walmart were recalled after 26 reports of them exploding or catching fire and 16 injuries, including second-degree burns (CPSC Ozark Trail). Health Canada noted 13 incidents in Canada from 2013 to 2021 and a 2017 recall (Health Canada butane).

## Cold

The gas pressure in a can follows its temperature: the colder the can, the lower the pressure and the weaker the flame (Jetboil FAQ). As the gas boils off, the can chills itself further (CPSC butane report).

| Gas | Boils at | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Butane (n-butane) | about 0 °C (32 °F) | Weak or dead near freezing, even indoors in an unheated house |
| Isobutane | about −11 °C (12 °F) | Boils lower than butane. Backpacking canisters pair it with propane (Jetboil FAQ); use only the can type your stove names |
| Propane | about −42 °C (−44 °F) | Still has pressure far below freezing; Jetboil blends it with isobutane for better cold performance (Jetboil FAQ) |

Boiling points from NIST (NIST butane, NIST isobutane, NIST propane). Read the can's label for what's in it. Jetboil says can pressure is directly proportional to temperature, so a can that has gone weak in the cold works better as it warms (Jetboil FAQ).

Warm a cold can with body heat only: inside your coat or in a sleeping bag between uses, then fit it just before you cook (Jetboil FAQ). Don't leave it sitting on snow or cold metal (Jetboil FAQ). Never warm a can with a flame, a stove top, a heater or by running a second burner near it. Makers warn heating it can make it explode (Jetboil Flash). Some cassette stoves have a metal plate built in that carries heat back to the can for cold-weather use; in CPSC's tests that model ran hottest of all when misused, so never add extra heat (CPSC butane report). Seals can also fail in the cold: Jetboil warns that below freezing an O-ring may not seal fully, which leaks fuel (Jetboil Flash), so check for leaks every time in winter.

## Indoors

In Canada these stoves come under the camp-stove standard, CSA/ANSI Z21.72 / CSA 11.2 (Health Canada butane). When CPSC reviewed that standard in 2003 it covered outdoor use only; a separate US outline for commercial butane stoves covered outdoors and indoor restaurant table cooking (CPSC butane report). CDC says never to use a portable camping stove inside a home, tent or camper (CDC power outage). Read your stove's label: if it says outdoor use only, take it outside.

People do cook indoors on these stoves, and in Hong Kong approved cassette cookers are household appliances. The conditions there are plain: a well-ventilated room with an exhaust fan running and doors or windows open, a stove checked before every use, and no use if it is rusty or damaged (HK CO case 2026). In July 2026 a man in Hong Kong was treated for carbon monoxide poisoning after cooking on an approved but badly rusted cassette cooker; the rust is believed to be the cause and no gas leak was found (HK CO case 2026). Any gas cooking puts CO and nitrogen dioxide into the room; Health Canada says to run the range hood fan, and to open a window close by if you have no hood (Health Canada cooking).

If your stove's label allows indoor use and you cook inside in an outage: open a window near the stove, keep a battery CO alarm in the room and one outside the sleeping area (Health Canada CO), cook in short sessions, and turn it off when the food is done. It is a cooker, not a heater. See [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors) for the other choices and [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide) for the alarm and symptoms.

## Cans

- Use the cans your stove names (Tiger cartridge stoves, EMSD cassette leaflet). Cassette cans are not the same as the threaded backpacking canisters.
- Never refill a disposable can, and never puncture or burn a used one (EMSD hot pot).
- Store cans upright in a dry, cool, ventilated place away from flames and heat (EMSD hot pot), never in a hot car or next to the stove. Take the can out of the stove when you finish (Jetboil Flash).
- Change cans with the stove off and cool, outside or by an open window, away from other flames and people (Jetboil Flash).
- US rules require the cans to pass a 55 °C (131 °F) hot-water test without leaking (CPSC butane report). That is a shipping test, not a safe working temperature for a can in a stove bay.

## When no help is coming

- **Flames from the canister bay, a roaring flame you can't turn down, or hissing:** turn the knob off only if you can reach it from the side in a second. Don't lift, tip or carry a burning stove (Jetboil Flash), and don't open the bay. Get everyone well back and out of line with the bay, and let it burn out. An overheated can either bursts or vents gas that catches fire (Health Canada butane), and the flames can shoot up 1.8 m (6 ft) (CPSC butane report).
- **Fire spreading to the table or room:** treat it as a gas-fed fire. Leave and close the door if it is more than a small fire you can smother; see [Fight or leave](#ref/reference_fire_heat/fight_or_leave).
- **Burns:** cool under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20, and cover loosely; see the [hot surfaces card](#browse/hazards/burn).
- **Headache, dizziness or nausea while cooking:** stove off, everyone into fresh air. See [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).
- **A stove that leaks, flares or is rusty after a fall, a fire or a winter in a damp shed:** take it out of use. Makers say never to use a leaking or damaged stove (Jetboil Flash), and a badly rusted cassette cooker is believed to have caused a CO poisoning in Hong Kong (HK CO case 2026).
- **Running out of cans:** the stove takes only its own cans (Tiger cartridge stoves). Cook outside on a propane or liquid-fuel stove (see [Liquid-fuel stoves and lanterns](#guides/skill_liquid_fuel_stove)), or on top of a vented wood stove.
